title: Across the Table
description: Familiar boards, useful rule distinctions and a few situations worth thinking through.

questions.prompt: How many squares are on a standard chessboard?
questions.explanation: Eight rows of eight squares make 64.

questions.prompt: Where are stones placed when playing Go?

choices.text: On intersections of the grid lines
In the centres of the squares

questions.hint: The grid marks positions rather than spaces to be filled.
questions.explanation: Go stones sit where horizontal and vertical lines meet, including the board’s edges and corners.

questions.prompt: In classic English-language Scrabble, what is a blank tile’s own point value?
questions.hint: The flexibility of the tile comes with a scoring trade-off.
questions.explanation: A blank has no letter points, whichever letter it represents. Word multipliers can still affect the word’s other points.

questions.prompt: In Othello, what happens to opposing discs directly trapped in a line between the disc you place and another of your discs?

choices.text: They are flipped to your colour
They move to the nearest corner
They score points but stay unchanged

questions.hint: A move changes ownership of pieces already on the board.
questions.explanation: All opposing discs outflanked by the move are turned over to show your colour.

questions.prompt: Under classic Monopoly rules, how many houses must be on each property of a complete colour group before its first hotel can be bought?
questions.hint: The rules require even development across the group, not just on one property.
questions.explanation: Each property must have four houses. A hotel then replaces the four houses on its own property.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Checked HOTELS and even-building rule in classic full-length rules, not optional short-game variation.

questions.prompt: In the 2020 CATAN base-game rules, a city is worth how many victory points in total?
questions.hint: An upgrade replaces the settlement; do not add the two buildings’ values together.
questions.explanation: A city is worth two victory points, compared with one for a settlement.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Checked base-game city value; asks total rather than points gained by upgrading.

questions.prompt: In classic English-language Scrabble, what bonus is awarded for using all seven rack tiles in one turn?
questions.hint: This bonus is added after calculating the score for the words formed.
questions.explanation: Using seven tiles in one turn adds a 50-point bonus to the word score.

questions.prompt: In classic Monopoly, a player lands on an unowned property and declines to buy it at the printed price. What happens next?

choices.text: The property is removed from the game
The bank offers it at auction
The next player receives it free
It becomes unavailable until the next round

questions.hint: The bank has a second way to sell property besides the printed-price purchase.
questions.explanation: The bank auctions it to the highest bidder. The player who declined the printed price may also bid.

questions.prompt: In standard chess, a player has no legal move but is not in check. What is the result?
questions.hint: Being unable to move is not, by itself, checkmate.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: FIDE2023 Article5.2.1; assumes the position arose legally.

questions.prompt: Using the 2020 CATAN base-game rules, you hold 9 resource cards when a 7 is rolled. How many must you discard, before any theft by the robber?
questions.hint: The discard applies only above the hand-size threshold, and half is rounded down.
questions.explanation: With more than seven resource cards, discard half rounded down: half of nine rounds down to four.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Checked printed rule p5; floor(9/2)=4. Development cards and later robber theft excluded explicitly.

questions.prompt: In the standard Pandemic base game, an unprevented infection would add a fourth cube of one colour to a city. What happens instead?

choices.text: Remove every cube from that city
Discover a cure for that colour
Place two cubes in that city
Trigger an outbreak from that city

questions.hint: The danger spreads through the network when a city reaches its local limit.
questions.explanation: An outbreak replaces the fourth cube: the outbreak marker advances, and connected cities receive that disease’s cubes.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Checked Infection and Outbreaks rules. Unprevented qualifier excludes role/event prevention; colour specified because a city can hold cubes of several colours.

questions.prompt: In standard backgammon scoring, how much is a gammon worth relative to the current value of the doubling cube?
questions.hint: A gammon is a stronger win than a single game, but differs from a backgammon.
questions.explanation: A gammon scores twice the cube value. A backgammon scores three times; a single game scores once.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Checked standard Gammons and Backgammons section; optional Jacoby rule excluded by standard scoring scope.

questions.prompt: Under the simple ko rule described by the British Go Association, what is forbidden immediately after a ko capture?

choices.text: Playing anywhere else on the board
Recapturing to recreate the position before that capture
Capturing stones in a different group

questions.hint: The rule prevents a local exchange from repeating without intervening play.
questions.explanation: Immediate ko recapture is forbidden. A player must first play elsewhere before that recapture becomes available.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Scoped to simple ko, not positional or situational superko; checked introductory ko example.

questions.prompt: In standard backgammon, a roll is 3 and 5. Either number can be played legally, but no sequence allows both to be used. What must the player do?
questions.hint: The rules limit the choice when part of a roll cannot be used.
questions.explanation: When either number alone is playable but both cannot be used, the larger number must be played.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Checked Movement of the Checkers rule4; both move orders excluded by wording, so no hidden legal sequence overrides the answer.

questions.prompt: Under the 2023 FIDE Laws, which condition makes an otherwise live game a draw when a player runs out of time?

choices.text: The opponent cannot force mate against best defence
The opponent has not yet given check
The opponent cannot mate by any legal sequence

questions.hint: Distinguish what can be forced from what is possible even with cooperative play.
questions.explanation: Article6.9 requires that no legal continuation could let the opponent checkmate. Merely lacking a forced mate is insufficient.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Checked Article6.9; live game excludes one already ended under Article5.
